title: What carries a historical shock to today's income, and does it fade?
text: It is unknown which channel carries a historical shock (the slave trade, the Scramble for Africa, colonial land tenure, the Holocaust, European settlement) into today's income and trust, and whether the legacy is a self-sustaining equilibrium or a slowly decaying shock. The field has established large reduced-form effects for each shock (Nunn 2008, Banerjee and Iyer 2005, Michalopoulos and Papaioannou 2016, Acemoglu et al. 2011) and a menu of candidate channels (state weakness, ethnic fractionalisation, human capital, a thinner middle class, cultural transmission, migrants' traits), but the authors themselves say the data cannot tell them apart.
why: A single shock moves every candidate channel at once and the intermediate outcomes (state capacity, trust, human capital at earlier dates) are rarely observed, so reduced-form designs cannot apportion the effect.

title: Which reformable institutions drive growth, separate from geography?
text: It is unknown which specific institutions (executive constraints, term limits, contracting versus property-rights rules, ethnic or local governance) drive growth, as opposed to institutional quality treated as one bundle, and how their effect can be separated from geography, climate, culture and prior development. The field has established a robust link between institutional quality and income and used colonial-origins and ethnic-border designs to read it as causal (Acemoglu et al. 2001, Michalopoulos and Papaioannou 2011), but the settler-mortality data are contested (Albouy 2010), the first stage weakens within Africa, and the ethnic-institution result is by its authors' account only a robust conditional correlation.
why: Institutions come as bundles and are measured by their outcomes rather than by the rules a policy maker could change (Glaeser et al. 2004), and no credible source of exogenous variation moves one rule at a time.

title: What changes inefficient institutions, and why do they outlast elites?
text: It is unknown what moves a society off inefficient institutions: how elite turnover, coalitions of social groups, non-voluntary change forced by excluded groups and reform backlash combine to decide whether elites, institutions or both change, and where institutions come from in the first place. The field has theory in which weak commitment, fear of replacement and failures of the political Coase theorem sustain inefficiency (Acemoglu 2003, Acemoglu and Robinson 2006, 2008), but the authors themselves say general models of institutional evolution are missing, coalitions and dynamics are sidestepped, and systematic tests (for example the early-18th-century capital-market evidence behind North and Weingast 1989) are still pending.
why: Institutions are endogenous, the forces the theories turn on (political competition, elites' attitudes, replacement threats, coalition bargaining) are barely measured, and the models are stylised two- or three-group set-ups with no systematic empirical counterpart.

title: How do informal norms, ideas and ideology interact with formal rules?
text: It is unknown how informal norms, conventions and ideology interact with formal laws and institutions, and whether ideas have an autonomous role in social change rather than merely reflecting material interests. The field has documented long-lived cultural traits such as trust and social capital (Nunn and Wantchekon 2011, Guiso et al. 2008) and modelled formal institutions in depth, but political-economy models still take preferences and constraints as given, and the authors flag conventions, social norms and ideas as under-studied (Young 1996, Rodrik 2015, Hwang et al. 2024, Acemoglu 2025).
why: Norms and worldviews are not recorded in historical or administrative data, and no variation shifts them independently of the formal rules and material interests they travel with.

title: Why did states form and build capacity so unevenly outside Europe?
text: It is unknown why states failed to emerge or to build capacity across much of the tropics, Africa and the Americas, and whether the war-driven, fiscal-capacity account built on European evidence, including conflict-driven mass schooling, travels beyond Europe, to democracies and to recent periods. The field has a rich body of state-formation theory and European evidence (Dincecco 2015, Paglayan 2022, Fernández-Villaverde et al. 2023), but the authors point to a very high ratio of theory to evidence, few systematic tests, and African states largely missing from the literature (Osafo-Kwaako and Robinson 2013, Abramson 2016, Herbst 2000).
why: Pre-colonial political and fiscal data outside Europe are sparse and possibly selected (for example the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample), which keeps theory far ahead of evidence.

title: Which land and property-rights reforms raise productivity, and how?
text: It is unknown which land and property-rights changes (tenancy reform, formal land rights, cooperative ownership, communal control) raise productivity and welfare, through what mechanism beyond investment and credit, and whether they beat alternatives such as credit or other asset transfers. The field has evidence from individual reforms (Banerjee et al. 2002, Field 2007, Montero 2021), but the authors call the evidence on mechanisms and on relative effectiveness thin, and note that the security and assignment of property rights are themselves endogenous (Besley and Ghatak 2010).
why: Large property-rights changes are rare outside social upheaval and the property-rights structure is itself endogenous, while the long panels and linked micro or administrative data that would reveal mechanisms are missing.

title: How do rural elites turn land and labour control into lasting power?
text: It is unknown through which levers (vote control, employment rents, labour coercion, chiefs' discretion, rent seeking) landed and local elites turn control of land and labour into persistent inequality and underdevelopment, and how much long-run damage runs through that political channel. The field has formal models and historical legacy estimates (Engerman and Sokoloff 2002, Dell 2010, Baland and Robinson 2008, Acemoglu and Wolitzky 2011), but results conflict across settings, with Latin American studies failing to find the expected negative long-run effect of land concentration (Naritomi et al. 2012), and the authors concede that direct evidence on rent seeking, chiefs' accountability or coercion is unavailable (Banerjee et al. 2001, Acemoglu et al. 2014).
why: Elite control works through informal levers that are rarely observed, so researchers can only test implications of specific mechanisms rather than measure vote control, rent seeking or accountability directly.

title: What makes elites concede democracy, and why do transitions cluster?
text: It is unknown what makes elites concede the franchise or lose power, how slow-moving forces (income, education, urbanisation, inequality) interact with the triggers (revolutionary threat, elite rivalry, coordination), and why democratic transitions cluster in time and across regions. The field has a strong cross-country income-democracy correlation that is contested once country fixed effects are included (Acemoglu et al. 2009) and well-studied episodes of reform under threat (Acemoglu and Robinson 2000, Aidt and Franck 2015, Fearon 2011), but the authors say a unified account is still lacking and the correlation and the clustering have been treated as distinct objects (Boix 2003, Abramson and Montero 2020, Treisman 2020).
why: Transitions are rare, the slow-moving drivers are endogenous and absorbed by country fixed effects, and the best-identified evidence comes from single episodes (such as Britain's 1832 reform) whose external validity is untested.

title: Which channels carry democracy's effects on growth and redistribution?
text: It is unknown through which channels and which specific features of democracy (competition, franchise, constraints, form of government, sequencing with liberalisation) shape growth, redistribution and the size of government, and whether a credible average effect of democracy can be estimated at all. The field has cross-country estimates of democracy's effects on growth, inequality and reform (Acemoglu et al. 2018, Papaioannou and Siourounis 2008, Spilimbergo et al. 2010) and evidence tying franchise extension to larger government (Berlinski et al. 2014, Husted and Kenny 1997), but the authors call the micro-level drivers a black box, 'democracy' too blunt a concept, and regime measures non-reproducible.
why: Few countries switch regime and overlap between treated and untreated is weak, regime measures are blunt and not reproducible, and the firm- and household-level data needed to trace channels are scarce.

title: Does democracy improve schooling and service quality, or the reverse?
text: It is unknown whether and how democratic competition improves the quantity and, above all, the quality of schooling, health and other services, through which mechanism (electoral competition, clientelism, information, decentralisation), and how much of the link runs the other way, with education building democracy or autocrats using it to stay in power. The field has associations and some evidence on specific cases, such as electoral competition and primary-school fees or democratisation and infant mortality (Harding and Stasavage 2013, Kudamatsu 2012), but the authors flag joint endogeneity and omitted time-varying factors behind regime and education (Stasavage 2005, Manzano 2017, Acemoglu et al. 2005) and thin evidence beyond primary schooling.
why: Regime and education are jointly determined by omitted time-varying factors, cross-country data on service inputs and quality are poor, and political decentralisation cannot be separated from democracy when instruments work through a broad cluster of institutions.

title: How do autocrats keep insiders and local agents loyal and productive?
text: It is unknown why some autocracies build durable institutions (ruling parties, legislatures, formal promotion rules) and select competent agents while others rule through purges and personal loyalty, and how much of what local agents deliver under promotion and quota systems is real rather than manipulated. The field has formal models of power-sharing, purges and coalition formation (Svolik 2009, Egorov and Sonin 2011, Gehlbach and Keefer 2011) and a growing body of evidence from China (Fisman and Wang 2017, Jia 2024, Meng et al. 2015), but the authors note little consensus on weakly institutionalised polities, no genuinely comparative study of authoritarian institutions (Gehlbach et al. 2016), and no account of why standard country characteristics fail to predict which autocracies perform (Besley and Kudamatsu 2008).
why: Autocrats' internal bargains are unobserved, official performance data can be gamed, and the evidence comes mostly from a few settings, chiefly China, so comparative tests of the models are missing.

title: How do media control and misinformation shape dissent and support?
text: It is unknown how rulers, parties and media shape citizens' beliefs and what that does to dissent and regime support: how subtle manipulation (fraud, media capture, targeted social control, repression, misinformation) works alongside formal institutions, how far the information environment is itself endogenous to the regime, and why simplistic or identity-driven beliefs take hold. The field has models of informational autocracy and misspecified beliefs (Guriev and Treisman 2015, 2018, Edmond 2013, Levy et al. 2022) and early evidence on the cost of opposition and the legacies of repression (Hsieh et al. 2011, Rozenas and Zhukov 2019), but the authors say regime control over information is taken as given and data on individuals' public political expression are scarce.
why: Preference falsification and exposure to propaganda are hard to observe, data on individuals' public political expression are scarce, and nothing shifts the information environment independently of the regime that controls it.

title: Do economic losses or cultural grievances drive populist support?
text: It is unknown which economic shocks (trade, austerity, financial crises, labour-market change) and which cultural or status grievances turn into populist and radical-right support, in which direction the causation runs, and who supplies populist politicians once demand exists. The field has established correlations between globalisation, austerity or crisis exposure and populist voting across US and European communities (Fetzer 2019, Funke et al. 2015, Broz et al. 2019), but the authors flag reverse causality from cultural to perceived economic grievances (Margalit 2019), no explanation of why globalisation rather than other shocks generates backlash (Rodrik 2021), and little evidence outside the West (Rydgren 2018).
why: Voters' subjective economic assessments and cultural identity are jointly determined, shocks such as trade, austerity and migration arrive together, and credible variation and data are largely confined to the US and Europe.

title: What links public support for democracy to its survival or erosion?
text: It is unknown how popular support for democracy translates into its survival or erosion: what citizens actually mean by democracy, why they tolerate norm-violating incumbents, whether supportive citizens act to defend institutions, how elected populists dismantle competitive elections and media freedom, and how extremist vote shares turn into breakdown. The field has models of voter responses to norm violation and of the conditions for liberal democracy (Grillo and Prato 2021, Mukand and Rodrik 2020), but the authors say how populist leaders dismantle institutions (Acemoglu et al. 2012) and how support affects survival (Acemoglu et al. 2024) are open, the micro-mechanisms need microdata on who benefits from democratic institutions, and the step from extremist vote shares to breakdown is not studied (de Bromhead et al. 2013).
why: Breakdowns are rare, citizens mean different things by democracy so 'support' is hard to compare, and the microdata on who benefits from democratic institutions that would identify the mechanisms do not exist.

title: Are voters instrumental, or expressive and socially motivated?
text: It is unknown how far voters act instrumentally (voting as if pivotal, abstaining or switching strategically, coordinating on likely winners) rather than expressively or under social pressure, and which competing turnout model best fits behaviour. The field has well-developed pivotal-voter, ethical and expressive models and some laboratory and field support (Coate et al. 2007, Battaglini et al. 2008, Fujiwara 2011, Funk 2010, Pons and Tricaud 2018), but the authors say direct tests are rare, costs, benefits and beliefs about being pivotal are unobservable in field data (Duffy and Tavits 2008), and a wide range of behaviour can be an equilibrium (Feddersen and Pesendorfer 1999).
why: Voting costs, benefits and beliefs about being pivotal are unobservable in field data, and equilibrium multiplicity lets many behaviours fit the theory, so no design cleanly separates instrumental from expressive motives.

title: How durable are the effects of mobilisation and enfranchisement?
text: It is unknown how long the effects of mobilisation, voting-access reforms and enfranchisement last, whether habits and social spillovers build on them, and who gains from them in resources and welfare. The field has many one-election field experiments and a few well-identified enfranchisement studies (Gerber et al. 2003, Cascio and Washington 2013, Naidu 2012, Cantoni and Pons 2019), but the authors say the magnitude and duration of voting habits, effects on later elections and on vote choice, and the long-run consequences for newly included groups remain unmeasured.
why: Most experiments measure only the next election, enfranchisement shocks are rare and work through slow channels such as the intergenerational transmission of human capital and wealth, and long individual-level voting panels are missing.

title: Does accountability select better politicians or discipline them?
text: It is unknown whether electoral accountability improves outcomes by selecting better types into office or by disciplining whoever holds it, and what that is worth in welfare terms, since term limits, term length, disclosure and debates move both at once. The field has natural experiments on term limits and tenure (Alt et al. 2011, Dal Bó and Rossi 2008, 2011) and field experiments on audits and report cards (Ferraz and Finan 2008, Banerjee et al. 2011), but the authors say the competence effect cannot be split into selection versus experience, welfare effects of turnover are unclear, and results from single natural experiments may not generalise.
why: Selection and discipline run through the same elections and the same treatments, separating them needs rare events such as incumbents surprised by a chance to run again, and welfare effects need outcome data that seldom exist.

title: Do information campaigns and media change accountability at scale?
text: It is unknown whether informing voters, through audits, report cards, debates, text messages or media, durably changes votes and politicians' behaviour once it is scaled up and politicians, parties and media respond, and through which channel (better-informed politicians, selection, salience, attention). The field has many short-run field experiments (Ferraz and Finan 2008, Banerjee et al. 2011, Bidwell et al. 2019, Bhandari et al. 2021) and models of media and attention (Matějka and Tabellini 2020, Prato and Wolton 2015), but the authors point to partial-equilibrium designs, unknown durability and external validity (Bobonis et al. 2016), and thin evidence on fake news, local media and media-market structure (Angelucci and Prat 2024, Larreguy et al. 2020).
why: Experiments are short, small and partial-equilibrium by design, the channels (information, salience, selection) are bundled in one treatment, and fine-grained data on media consumption and politicians' responses are missing.

title: When do voters reward delivery, via which channel, and for how long?
text: It is unknown when and why voters reward governments for visible delivery (cash transfers, roads, schools, services) rather than ignoring or punishing it, whether any reward comes from gratitude, salience, implementation quality or credit claiming, and whether it lasts once programmes become routine. The field has well-identified single-programme estimates, mostly positive (La O 2012, Manacorda et al. 2009, Zucco 2013), but the authors report nulls and reversals elsewhere (Goyal 2023, de Kadt and Lieberman 2017), cannot separate quality from salience (Zimmermann 2020, Bueno et al. 2023), rely on aggregate data (Ajzenman and Durante 2019), and flag unknown external validity and medium-run effects.
why: Transfers, roads and services reach voters together with campaigns, brokers and other benefits, so gratitude, salience, credit claiming and quality cannot be separated, and most estimates are aggregate and cover one programme over a few elections.

title: What do electoral targeting and timed spending cost in welfare?
text: It is unknown what electorally motivated allocation costs in welfare against rule-based allocation: whether targeting of services, utility supply and enforcement forbearance, and spending timed to elections, outweighs the gains from better-informed local targeting, and which strategy (core, swing, broker clientelism, programmatic infrastructure) parties pick under which competitive conditions. The field has well-documented patterns of targeting aligned and swing areas (Dixit and Londregan 1996, Callen et al. 2019, Mahadevan and Shenoy 2023), forbearance toward the poor (Holland 2014, 2017) and budget cycles that shrink as democracies gain experience (Akhmedov and Zhuravskaya 2004, Brender and Drazen 2005), but the authors say net welfare, the cost of political capture and the returns to programmatic versus targeted strategies are unmeasured.
why: The rule-based counterfactual is never observed, programmes mix technical and electoral aims, and the data on losses, service quality, enforcement and pre-election activity that would price the distortion are scarce.

title: Why leaders favor co-ethnics and which institutions or ties curb it
text: It is unknown why leaders favor their own ethnic group and through which channels, how much of that is electoral exchange rather than altruism toward co-ethnics, and which institutions, cleavage structures and party systems curb favoritism or switch off ethnic voting. The field has robust evidence that co-ethnic leaders deliver more roads, schools, health services and nighttime light to their own group (Franck and Rainer 2012, Burgess et al. 2015, Hodler and Raschky 2014), that multiparty democracy reduced it in Kenya, and that cross-cutting ties weaken ethnic voting in Mali (Dunning and Harrison 2010), but the authors say the mechanisms, the link to growth and the conditions under which ethnicity becomes the basis of voting are open.
why: Spending data by ethnic group are scarce, observational patterns cannot separate quid pro quo from altruism or electoral targeting, and the evidence rests on single settings (Kenya, Malawi, Mali, India) that may not travel.

title: Where electoral rules come from, when they are the rules that matter
text: A set of mostly theoretical papers treats electoral rules as endogenous - chosen by the actors they will govern - rather than as the exogenous institution the empirical literature usually assumes. What is unknown is which rules get chosen under what conditions, and how much of the measured effect of a rule is really the effect of whatever made it adoptable.
why: The rules are endogenous and rarely change, so there is little exogenous variation to exploit and almost no empirical work behind the theory.
